David never said that the pain went away. But he showed what a person can do when life asks for the impossible: take the next step, and then the one after that.

Most of us will never face anything like this. So when we feel overwhelmed by our own troubles, David's story gives us a gentle thought. We are stronger than we believe, and there is always a way to go on.
source: Wikipedia, Murder of the Hatuel family

title: One Eye on the Road
text:
The story goes that Moshe Dayan, the famous Israeli general who wore a black patch over one eye, was once stopped for speeding.

The policeman recognized him at once. "General," he said, "someone like you should set an example for everyone else. I have to give you a ticket."

Dayan looked at him calmly. "Officer, you can see that I have only one eye. So tell me, which should I keep it on, the speedometer or the road?"

It is a funny answer, and it holds a real lesson. Many of us keep our eyes so tightly on the speedometer, on how fast we are going and how we measure up, that we forget to look at the road ahead.

How we are getting there matters. But where we are going matters even more. Once in a while, it is worth lifting our eyes and asking whether we are heading somewhere that we truly want to reach. A little time spent on that question can save a lot of wandering.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: The Elephant and the Small Chain
text:
Have you ever watched a circus elephant? It weighs several tons, yet it stands patiently, held by a thin chain tied to a small wooden stake. With one step, it could snap the chain and walk away. Why doesn't it?

The tale explains it this way. When the elephant was a baby, it was tied with the very same chain. It pulled and pulled, with all its little might, but the stake did not budge. After many days of trying, it gave up.

And then something quiet happened. The elephant came to believe that the chain could not be broken. It grew into a giant, but the memory of those early failures stayed with it. It no longer tests the chain, because it is certain the answer is no.

How many of us are tied to a small stake like that? Something we tried when we were young, or when we were less ready, did not work out, and we decided we could never do it. Perhaps it was learning to pray, to keep Shabbat, to forgive, or to change.

Our Sages teach that a person is never too old to begin, and never too weak to try again. Give the chain one more pull. You may be stronger than you think.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: The City Without Water
text:
About five hundred years ago, the Mughal emperor Akbar the Great decided to build a new capital in northern India. He chose a site called Fatehpur Sikri and spent a fortune on it.

The city was breathtaking. It had palaces, courtyards, gardens and great halls, built of red sandstone and marble, blending the best of Persian and Hindu design.

But the court lived there for only about fourteen years. According to many historians, the city simply did not have enough water. Whatever the exact reasons, the emperor and his court left, and the magnificent capital was abandoned.

Today Fatehpur Sikri is one of the most visited sites in India. It stands there, beautiful and silent, a city with everything except what it needed most.

Our Sages compare Torah to water. Without water, nothing can live, no matter how impressive it looks. A Jewish life, a family or a community can have wonderful buildings, successes and plans. But without the quiet, steady flow of Torah to nourish it, it cannot last.

The good news is that this water is free and always near. A few minutes of learning each day, a Shabbat meal, a blessing said with a smile: these are how we keep our own city alive.

title: The Woman Who Searched for Herself
text:
In August 2012, a bus full of tourists stopped near a volcanic canyon in Iceland called Eldgja. When they got back on board, the guide counted heads and found one passenger missing.

The police were alerted, and about fifty people set out in the dark to look for her. A rescue helicopter was grounded by fog, so the tourists searched on foot. The description they were given was of a woman in dark clothes.

One of the searchers was a tourist who had changed her clothes since the stop. She did not recognize herself in the description, so she joined the search with everyone else.

Hours passed, until around three in the morning it finally became clear that the missing woman was not missing at all. She had been looking for herself the whole night.

It is a funny story, but it has a serious side. Many of us spend years searching for something, meaning, belonging, our place, without realizing that we are the one we have been looking for.

Our teachers say that every Jew carries a deep, holy soul that never goes missing. It may be dressed in different clothes, so that we hardly recognize it. But it is always there, and we can find it at any moment, especially in the days of return before Yom Kippur.

title: You Know the Psalm, I Know the Shepherd
text:
At a concert, a world-famous singer was asked to perform Psalm 23, "The Lord is my shepherd." He sang it magnificently. His voice soared, every note was perfect, and the audience rose to its feet with thunderous applause.

Then an old Jewish man in the back stood up. He did not have a polished voice. It was rough and cracked, and he stumbled over a few words. But as he recited the psalm, people began to cry. By the end, the whole room was in tears.

Afterward, the singer came over to him, puzzled. "I don't understand," he said. "I sang it beautifully, and they applauded. You sang it, and they wept. What is the difference?"

The old man smiled gently. "It is simple," he said. "You know the psalm. I know the Shepherd."

Our prayers do not need a beautiful voice or perfect pronunciation. What opens hearts, our own and others', is how close we feel to the One we are talking to. When we pray like a child speaking to a loving parent, even a few simple words can reach all the way to heaven.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: The Deaf Husband and the Blind Wife
text:
The story is told of a couple who had been happily married for many years, though on the surface they seemed a poor match.

The husband was far from handsome, and his wife was a sharp-tongued woman who complained from morning to night. But the wife was blind, and the husband was deaf. She pictured a tall, handsome man at her side. And whenever she grumbled, he imagined she was saying something sweet.

One day the husband read about a doctor who could cure even the most serious impairments. "Let's go," they agreed. "Why live with less than we could have?"

The operations were a complete success. The husband could hear, and the wife could see.

And their marriage fell apart within weeks. She saw the husband she had actually married, and he finally heard what she had actually been saying.

The tale is a smile with a serious point. We often think, "If only my situation were different, everything would be better." But life is not always improved by changing our circumstances. G-d gave each of us particular strengths and weaknesses. Our work is to make the best of what we have, and to look kindly at the people around us, flaws and all.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: I Am Jealous of You
text:
Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev was known as the great defender of the Jewish people. He always looked for the good in everyone.

One day he met a man in town who was known for living far from Torah and mitzvot, and who seemed to take pride in it. The Rebbe looked at him warmly and said, "I am jealous of you."

The man was shocked. "Jealous of me? Why?"

"Because of what you will have when you do teshuvah, when you return," said the Rebbe. "When someone comes back to G-d out of love, our Sages teach that even the wrong things he did can be turned into merits. Think of how much good you will have to your name. I have never had the chance to turn so much around."

The man had expected a lecture. Instead he had been told that nothing in his past could shut the door. That the whole of his life, even the broken parts, could become light.

That is the Chassidic view of every Jew. Nobody is beyond reach, nobody is a lost cause, and a past full of mistakes is not a wall but raw material. When we return with love, G-d does not only forgive. He helps us transform.

It is a message especially for the days before Yom Kippur, but it is true all year round.

title: The Last House He Built
text:
Moshe was a master builder. Everything he built stood tall and strong, and people came from far away to praise his work.

When he was ready to retire, he told his boss, the contractor, that he was looking forward to a long, well-earned vacation with his wife. But on his very last week, the contractor came to him with one more request. “Just one more house, Moshe. There is no one I trust like you.”

Moshe agreed, but his heart was already on the vacation. For the first time in his life he cut corners. He measured carelessly, used poor materials and rushed to finish. The house he put up was full of cracks and creaks, the kind that would not last through a storm.

When it was done, the contractor shook his hand. “Moshe, you have given me many years of wonderful work. This house is my gift to you.” And he handed him the key.

Moshe had built his own home.

Our Sages teach that the way we treat others comes back to us. The care we give to our parents, our family and our community is the house we will one day live in.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: Good Morning, Herr Mueller
text:
Before the war, a Chassidic rabbi in Poland loved to greet everyone he met. On his daily walk he would pass a neighbor named Herr Mueller, tip his hat and say warmly, “Good morning, Herr Mueller!” Mueller, who was proud to be greeted so respectfully by the rabbi, would answer, “Good morning, Herr Rabbiner!”

Then the war came. The walks stopped. Friends turned away, neighbors disappeared, and Mueller put on the uniform of the Nazis.

Years later, in Auschwitz, the rabbi stood in a line of prisoners waiting to be sorted. One gesture of an officer’s hand sent a person to the left, to death, and another to the right, to life. The rabbi was old and weak, and he knew very well which way his hand would point.

When he reached the front, he looked up and saw the officer’s face. It was Herr Mueller.

The rabbi stood straight, as he always had, and softly said, “Good morning, Herr Mueller.”

The officer froze. Then, very quietly, he answered, “Good morning, Herr Rabbiner.” And his hand pointed to the right.

The story comes from Yaffa Eliach’s collection of Chassidic tales of the Holocaust, who wrote it down from an elderly Chassidic man. It reminds us that a simple greeting, given every day, never goes to waste.
source: Hasidic Tales of the Holocaust by Yaffa Eliach (also retold on Breslev.co.il)

title: The Cat Is on the Roof
text:
Phil had never taken a day off in his life. He cared for his elderly mother and his beloved cat, and finally his family convinced him to take a long vacation. His brother promised to look after both.

On the first day, Phil called to ask about the cat. “I’m so sorry,” said his brother. “The cat died. It ran into the street.”

Phil was heartbroken. “You have to learn how to tell people bad news,” he said. “You could have prepared me. First you say, ‘The cat is on the roof.’ The next day, ‘We’re having trouble getting the cat down.’ The day after, ‘I’m sorry, the cat fell.’ That way I would have known something was coming.”

His brother apologized and promised to do better.

“Now,” said Phil, “how is Mom?”

There was a long pause. “Well,” said his brother, “Mom is on the roof.”

The lesson: kindness matters, but so does clarity. If we are so careful not to speak directly that no one understands us, we do not help anyone. Speak gently, but speak honestly.

title: The Two Yuds
text:
A little boy had just started learning Chumash, the Five Books of Moses, in cheder, the traditional Jewish school. He had been taught that two letters yud written together stand for Hashem’s holy name, and so whenever he saw them, he would say “Hashem.”

One day, reading aloud, he ended every verse with “Hashem.” The teacher stopped him. “Why do you say that?”

The boy pointed. “Look, Rebbe. At the end of every verse there are two yuds!” He was seeing the two dots, like a colon, that mark the end of a verse.

The teacher smiled. Those dots are not G-d’s name, he explained, but the boy had noticed something wonderful. A yud can also stand for a Yid, a Jew. When two Jews stand side by side, as friends and equals, G-d’s presence rests between them. But when one stands above the other, looking down on his friend, the two yuds are just the end of the verse. The shining stops.

The story is told in Chassidic tradition, often in the name of Rabbi Naftali of Ropshitz, who taught that where there is true unity, there is G-d.
source: Chabad.org (“Harmony”), a story told in Chassidic tradition

title: Write It in Sand, Carve It in Stone
text:
Two friends were walking through the desert. Somewhere along the way they began to argue, and one of them struck the other across the face.

The one who was hit said nothing. He knelt and wrote in the sand: “Today my best friend hit me.”

They walked on until they reached an oasis and went in to bathe. The friend who had been hit got stuck in the mud and began to sink. The other friend pulled him out and saved his life.

When he had recovered, he took a stone and carved: “Today my best friend saved my life.”

The friend who had struck him asked, “Why did you write the first in sand and the second in stone?”

He answered, “When someone hurts us, we should write it in sand, where the winds of forgiveness can blow it away. But when someone does us good, we should carve it in stone, where no wind can erase it.”

The Torah asks us to love our neighbor and not to hold a grudge. This story shows how: let the hurts fade, and remember the kindness.

title: The Boy With the Books
text:
One Friday, a high school freshman noticed a classmate named Kyle walking home carrying every book he owned. “What a nerd,” he thought, and kept walking.

Then he saw a group of boys knock the books out of Kyle’s arms and send him sprawling in the dirt. His glasses flew into the grass. The freshman saw the sadness in Kyle’s eyes, ran over, helped him find his glasses and picked up the books. They talked all the way home. Kyle turned out to be funny and kind, and the two became best friends.

Years later, at graduation, Kyle stood up as the top student of the class to give his speech. He thanked his parents and teachers, and then said that the best gift is to be a friend. He told the story of the day they met. He had planned to take his own life that weekend, which is why he was taking his things home. One kind boy, who just stopped to help, had changed his mind.

The friend stared. He had never known.

The story reminds us that a small act of kindness can change a life, and that we rarely know how much it matters. Our Sages say that saving one life is like saving an entire world. Often it begins by simply stopping to help.

If you or someone you love is struggling, please reach out to someone you trust. The Rabbi is always here to listen.

title: Be a Player, Not a Fan
text:
In 1955, a boy about to become Bar Mitzvah came with his father to see the Lubavitcher Rebbe at 770 Eastern Parkway in Brooklyn. In those years, boys often met the Rebbe privately before their Bar Mitzvah to receive a blessing.

The Rebbe asked about his birthday, tested him on what he was studying, and gave him a blessing. Then he surprised everyone. “Are you a baseball fan?”

The boy said he was, and that he rooted for the Dodgers. The Rebbe asked whether he went to games. Yes, the boy said, a month ago. “How was it?” Disappointing, he admitted. By the sixth inning the Dodgers were losing nine to two, so they left.

“Did the players leave also?” asked the Rebbe.

The boy was startled. “Of course not. The players can’t leave in the middle of the game!”

“Why not?”

“Because they are in the game. Fans can leave whenever they like. The players have to stay until the end and keep trying to win.”

The Rebbe smiled. “In the game of life, there are two kinds of people. Some watch from the stands, and some play. Take this lesson with you: be a player.”

The story is told on Chabad.org.

title: The Brick and the Jaguar
text:
A successful young executive was driving through a quiet neighborhood in his brand-new Jaguar, a little too fast. He watched for children darting out between parked cars. None appeared. But suddenly a brick slammed into the side door.

He slammed on the brakes, backed up and jumped out. He grabbed the first boy he saw and pushed him against a car. “What are you doing? That’s a new car, and that brick will cost a fortune!”

“Please, mister, I’m sorry,” the boy said, with tears running down his face. “I didn’t know what else to do. No one would stop.” He pointed. “It’s my brother. He rolled off the curb and fell out of his wheelchair, and I can’t lift him. Please, can you help?”

The man swallowed hard. He lifted the boy’s brother back into the chair, wiped his scrapes with a handkerchief and made sure he was all right. “Thank you, and G-d bless you,” the boy said.

The man watched them walk home. It was a long, slow walk back to his car. He never fixed the dent. It reminded him not to go through life so fast that someone has to throw a brick to get his attention.

Sometimes G-d whispers to us. When we don’t listen, we may hear Him in a louder way.

title: A Shofar for the Children
text:
This story is told every year before Rosh Hashanah. It is a hard story, and it is told with great respect.

It is said that on the eve of Rosh Hashanah in Auschwitz, a group of Jewish children sat huddled in their barracks, whispering. They knew what lay ahead. One of them, perhaps only eight years old, said, “Tomorrow is Rosh Hashanah. We must hear the shofar before it is too late.”

A message was passed in secret to the men’s barracks, where a rabbi had managed to hide a shofar. The next morning, at great risk, the rabbi came and blew it for the children.

When the last note faded, one of the children said, “Rabbi, we want you to know that we will die believing in G-d.”

The story is told on Chabad.org and elsewhere, but without names or dates, and we cannot confirm it. It is told to remind us of the pure faith of Jewish children, and of the parents and teachers who gave it to them. Whatever each of us believes, we are asked to listen to the shofar, and to remember.

title: The Minister of Defence
text:
When Margaret Thatcher was Britain’s Secretary of State for Education, she met the Chief Rabbi of the United Kingdom, Rabbi Immanuel Jakobovits. In the conversation, he told her something she never forgot: “You are really the Minister of Defence.”

He explained what he meant. After what children learn at home, it is what they learn in school that keeps a nation whole and strong.

Years later, in 1991, she recalled the remark in a speech at a dinner honoring Rabbi Jakobovits on his retirement as Chief Rabbi. She said it carried special meaning for the Jewish people. The Jews are a small people, scattered across the world. Where other nations relied on armies and statecraft to survive, the Jewish people relied mainly on learning. Education has been our greatest defense.

That is why a Jewish child learning the alef-bet, a family around the Shabbat table, and a Hebrew school class in Lafayette, Moraga or Orinda are not small things. They are how the Jewish people has always protected its future.
source: Margaret Thatcher’s speech at Rabbi Jakobovits’ retirement dinner (margaretthatcher.org), also reported by JTA
